A `/converge` run's return names three kinds of judgment its agents make without the owner only as counts, or not at all, so an owner who disagrees with one cannot find it from the run's report, though [story:veto-calls-made-in-my-absence](.ok-planner/design/stories/veto-calls-made-in-my-absence.md) promises 'a way to see every call made while I was away, so that I can overturn one I disagree with'.

The three judgments are these. A fixer declines a defect, and a verifier accepts the decline. A merge agent sorts a driver's failure `not-owed` on its one reading of what the product owes. A merge agent rejects a hunter's or a sprint pass's report as not real, or as a harm the accept list does not cover ([converge/prompts/merge.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/merge.md#L19-L20)). Each agent writes its reason as a note in the run's task ledger under `.ok-planner/review/runs/`. The return ([converge/SKILL.md:The return](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L146-L150)) counts declines on its `fixed` line and counts not-owed and rejected failures on its `hunt` line. Its `intake` line lists rejections only where the file is a record or a document the release regenerates. To overturn any other judgment, the owner must read the ledger.

The run already surfaces a judgment its agent was unsure of: a merge that sees two readings of what the product owes records a question call, and the owner list files it into the intake. A stuck defect becomes a judgment issue. In sprint mode an `unlisted` call goes to the completion report, which records 'what was decided in the owner's absence' for a sprint execution ([concept:completion-report](.ok-planner/design/concepts/completion-report.md)). The gap is a judgment an agent made with confidence: nothing lists it by site and reason.

The corpus never defines 'call', so the story reads two ways: every judgment an agent makes alone, or only what the suite records as a call (the calls pool's items, triage's rulings and closes, a builder's calls). [decision:skill-text-is-reviewed-as-code](.ok-planner/design/decisions/skill-text-is-reviewed-as-code.md) names a fixer that declines a fix apart from one that records a question, and [decision:converge-finds-then-fixes](.ok-planner/design/decisions/converge-finds-then-fixes.md) lets a defect end 'declined with a reason a verifier accepts' without saying whether that decline is a call.

The ruling decides whether each decline, not-owed sort, and report rejection a run makes alone must reach the owner by site and reason.

recommendation.text:
Treat every judgment a `/converge` run makes without the owner as a call the owner can veto. The run's return lists each verified decline, each failure sorted not-owed on one reading, and each report rejected as not real or not covered, one line each with its site and its reason, beside the ledger's path. The counts stay as the summary above those lines.

Rationale: the story promises every call made while the owner was away, and the suite already treats a dismissal made without the owner as one to veto: `/triage-issues` lists each issue it answers or retires in its report for veto, and [decision:closed-issues-leave-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/decisions/closed-issues-leave-new-analysis.md) relies on a close naming its reason so that a person can veto it. A merge's rejection or not-owed sort is the same act as triage's retire: it dismisses a claim. A not-owed sort judges what the product owes, the judgment the owner most needs to see, so option C hides the wrong half, and option B makes every veto a ledger read. Option A adds one line per judgment. Flip case: if analysis runs routinely reject hundreds of reports, so that the return stops being readable, the return lists declines and not-owed sorts and points to one file that lists every rejection, which still keeps each call findable from the report.

title: A /converge run's declines, not-owed sorts, and report rejections reach the owner only as counts

problem:
A drive of this project never exercises the dashboard's page, because no driver session carries a browser tool, so the page's controls go untested on every run. [decision:drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user](.ok-planner/design/decisions/drive-tries-each-story-as-a-user.md) has a driver try 'every surface the story is offered through', and [decision:local-web-surface](.ok-planner/design/decisions/local-web-surface.md) makes the dashboard a page because working the intake needs 'keys to move through the queue and rule without leaving it'. The mechanism: the drive prompt tells a driver, where a surface runs in a browser, to 'open a page of your own with `new_page`' ([converge/prompts/drive.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/drive.md#L17)), and names no path for a session without that tool. This project has no `.mcp.json`, so no session carries a browser MCP server. The page is a client-rendered shell, `
` on `GET /`, so only a browser exercises its controls; `curl` reaches only the JSON routes the page calls. The dashboard's drive steps already allow that substitute: step 3 reads 'Drive the page at the service's address, or its JSON routes with `curl`' ([.ok-planner/review/project.md](.ok-planner/review/project.md#L82)). In run converge-2026-10-16T040507 a driver did so: every `POST /api/issue//rule` answered 200, [story:rule-on-the-whole-intake](.ok-planner/design/stories/rule-on-the-whole-intake.md) passed over the routes, and the page's rule keys went undriven. The owner reads a pass that never touched the page. The state of play: the routes are driven, the page is not, and nothing reports the gap. The `/setup-web` skill of the suite's ok-web plugin merges the chrome-devtools MCP server into a project's `.mcp.json`, which gives every session `new_page`. No stated rule decides among the options. The ruling decides what changes so that a drive reaches the page, or reports that it could not.

recommendation.text:
Wire the chrome-devtools MCP server into this project with `/setup-web`, and change the drive prompt so a driver whose surface needs a browser, in a session with no browser tool, records that surface blocked with the reason instead of standing another surface in for it. The dashboard's drive steps then name the page as the surface the story is driven through, and the JSON routes no longer stand in for it.

Rationale: the page is a surface the story is offered through, and its keys are the reason the dashboard is a page rather than a terminal report, so a drive that stops at the routes skips the part the dashboard exists for; only wiring the browser tool (A) closes that gap here. The drive prompt change (C) serves every project the suite ships to: without it, a consumer whose drivers lack a browser tool reads a pass over a page nobody drove, the same false pass this run produced. A statement in the review facts (B) records the gap in one project and leaves the page untested. The flip case: if the machines that run drives cannot install Chrome, A is out, and C with B's statement in the review facts is the right pair.

title: Drivers cannot drive the dashboard's page because no driver session has a browser tool

problem:
When the owner drops a document type whose target is a single file, `/document` leaves that type's last document at its target, stamped with an older release, and the run's own goal then fails on it in this release and every later one. That breaks [story:ship-release-documents](.ok-planner/design/stories/ship-release-documents.md), which promises readers 'documentation that describes that release'.

The documentation walk proposes dropping a declared type whose covered classes returned no public element ([document/SKILL.md:Empty types](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L132)). Placement then writes only declared targets: 'no path is touched that no type names' ([document/SKILL.md:Placement](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L312)). Under a folder target, Placement removes every stamped document no declared type produced this release, 'so a document whose type was dropped does not linger' ([document/SKILL.md:Placement](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L314)). No step does the same for a file target. So the dropped type's document stays where readers look, and [document/goal.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/goal.md#L83-L87) lists 'a document at a path no type targets' under Not met. The run may not touch that path, so the goal never verifies. The next walk raises the file as untyped documentation ([document/SKILL.md:Untyped documentation](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L133)), but its 'drops the file as not documentation' removes nothing either, so only a hand deletion clears it.

A drive in run converge-2026-10-16T040507, the sprint certification of [the stack helpers sprint](.ok-planner/sprints/2026-10-15-stack-helpers.md), found it, and a merge agent confirmed it as real and outside that sprint's scope. Accept-list entry [A3](.ok-planner/review/catalog/accept.md#L11) covers it: an owner's action through a shipped verb leaves a state where later runs fail.

The fix needs a choice, because [decision:documents-generated-per-type-and-placed](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documents-generated-per-type-and-placed.md) commits that 'only declared types' targets are written' and that 'nothing is overwritten that no type claims'. The same decision already allows one removal: the documentation folder's rules file, which the ceremony removes once no type targets that folder. Folder targets are handled; file targets are not.

The ruling decides whether dropping a file-target type removes its stamped document, on the drop alone or on the owner's separate word.

recommendation.text:
Dropping a file-target type removes the document the ceremony wrote at its target, in the same run, where that document opens with the ceremony's provenance stamp. A file at the target with no stamp is hand-kept and stays. The commitment that the ceremony writes only declared types' targets gains this one removal, beside the removal of the documentation folder's rules file it already allows.

Rationale: the ceremony already removes a dropped type's stamped document under a folder target, so that it does not linger; option A gives a file target the same treatment, and one rule then covers both target shapes. The stamp keeps placement safe: it proves the ceremony wrote the file, and a placed document is a record the next release regenerates whole ([decision:placed-documents-are-records](.ok-planner/design/decisions/placed-documents-are-records.md)), so removing it loses nothing the owner wrote. The owner's drop in the walk is the consent. Option B asks a second time for the same act, and where the owner keeps the file it leaves a stamped orphan the next walk raises again. Option C makes the goal pass while readers still meet an older release's document. Flip case: if owners drop a type to stop regenerating a document they mean to keep by hand, the drop no longer implies removal, and option B, which asks, is the better rule.

options.label: A
options.text: Keep lending: the run's group owns the terminal while its command runs, so Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z act on the whole run as they act on a shell's foreground job. Cost: a Ctrl-C also ends a background server the operator meant to keep until `stop`.

options.label: B
options.text: Refuse a terminal: `run-group start` refuses where its input, output, or error is a terminal, or runs the command with input from `/dev/null`, so a run's command always runs apart from the operator's terminal. Cost: an interactive command, such as a prompt or a password read, cannot run under run-group, and an operator who runs it by hand must redirect.

options.label: C
options.text: Lend no terminal: the command stays in the run's group, Ctrl-C reaches run-group alone, and run-group forwards SIGINT to the command's own process, so background members run until `stop`. Cost: a command that reads the terminal stops on SIGTTIN, and the forwarding handler is new code.

problem:
When an operator runs `run-group start` at a terminal, it lends the terminal to the run's whole process group, so a Ctrl-C meant for the foreground command also ends every background server the command started. The corpus fixes that every process a run starts sits in the run's process group, and says nothing of what an operator's keystrokes reach.

The mechanism: `start` ([run-group:start](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L309)) asks [run-group:foreground_terminal](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L249) whether its input, output, or error is a terminal whose foreground group is run-group's own. Where one is, [run-group:run_lent](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L296) hands the terminal to the run's group while the command runs, and [run-group:lent_wait](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L279) takes it back when the command exits, and stops run-group itself when the command stops for any reason but a terminal read, so Ctrl-Z stops run-group as a shell job stops. The holder process that leads the group ignores SIGINT, SIGQUIT, and SIGTSTP ([run-group:HOLD_CODE](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/run-group#L66)), so the group outlives a Ctrl-C. A server the command starts with a trailing `&` stays in the group, because `stop` signals the group, so it receives the operator's SIGINT too unless it ignores that signal. The reference doc states this behavior ([docs/stack-helpers.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/stack-helpers.md#L214-L221)). The reference stack tool never meets it, since it runs the start command with input from `/dev/null` and its output to a log ([scripts/stack](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/stack#L489)). An operator who runs `run-group start` by hand meets it, and so does a project's own command that calls it at a terminal.

The state of play: [decision:stack-helpers-serve-project-commands](.ok-planner/design/decisions/stack-helpers-serve-project-commands.md) ships run-group as a helper a project may call from its own commands, 'each usable alone', and [decision:run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run](.ok-planner/design/decisions/run-artifacts-removed-with-the-run.md) has `down` stop 'the run's process group'. Running the command outside the run's group would break `stop`, so that reading is no option. No accept-list entry decides the terminal. A choice other than the built one edits the reference doc and run-group's entry in this project's review facts in the same change.

The ruling decides what a run's process group owes an operator at a terminal.

recommendation.text:
Keep lending the terminal to the run's group. While a run's command runs at an operator's terminal, Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Z act on every process of the run but the holder, as they act on a shell's foreground job, and `stop` still removes whatever is left.

Rationale: the corpus makes the run's process group the unit a run is stopped by, so a keystroke that acts on the whole group treats the run as the one thing the corpus says it is; an operator who stops a run's foreground step at a terminal expects the run to stop, not to leave servers running whose only trace is the group. Lending (A) matches the job control every shell user already knows, which suits a helper the corpus ships to be usable alone, and it is built and documented. Refusing a terminal (B) takes away interactive commands to limit a keystroke's reach, and lending no terminal (C) adds a forwarding handler and stops any command that reads the terminal. The flip case: if projects' own commands call `run-group start` at a terminal as a development loop, where the operator ends a foreground step such as a log tail and expects the server to keep running, C fits that use and earns its handler.

title: run-group start lends the operator's terminal to the whole run, so Ctrl-C also ends the run's background servers

options.label: A
options.text: Completeness relative to the extraction: the catalog matches the extraction's public side one-to-one, as the documentation skill already says, the surface extraction concept says the walk's exhaustiveness is not promised, and the story is narrowed to say so. Cost: the story's confidence 'without reading the source' rests on a walk nobody can refute.

options.label: B
options.text: Exhaustive enumeration: the extractor records, per kind, the source it enumerated from (the files, registries, or declarations it read) and the count it found there, commits to enumerating every member of that source, and the catalog's population rests on that record, so a later audit can re-enumerate the source and refute a missed element. Cost: the concept's 'nothing else' boundary widens, the extractor's 'no deeper than classification requires' bound changes, and each audit run costs more.

options.label: C
options.text: A named source with no promise: the extractor names, per kind, the source its walk read, in the shape of the audit's count-and-population rule, the concept says only that, and the story reads as completeness relative to the walk. Cost: a reader can check absence against a named source, and nothing promises the source holds every member.

problem:
The documentation catalog counts each public kind against the audit's surface extraction, and the extraction records no population it enumerated from, so an element the audit's walk missed reads as one that does not exist. [story:answer-absence-from-catalogs](.ok-planner/design/stories/answer-absence-from-catalogs.md) promises an agent consuming a release 'every declared user-facing surface kind cataloged completely over its enumerated population', so that it can answer 'does this capability exist?' with confidence from the catalog alone, without reading the source.

The mechanism: the audit dispatches a surface extractor that walks the code and the deployment configuration and writes one entry per element the walk found, each kind discovered by the walk and never pre-declared ([audit/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L99)). The extractor's rules bound the walk, which 'goes no deeper than classification requires', and ask for no per-kind source or count ([audit/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/audit/SKILL.md#L103-L105)). `/document` then writes one catalog file per kind whose `population:` is the count of public members the extraction holds, with rows that 'match the extraction's public side one-to-one' ([document/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L164-L168)), and tells the reader that 'what is not in the catalog does not exist' ([document/SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/document/SKILL.md#L18)). The catalog's completeness is checked only against the extraction, so nothing a later reader or audit holds can refute an omission the walk made. The agent that consumes the release sees the harm: it answers 'does not exist' with false confidence.

The state of play: the story's 'enumerated population' reads two ways, as the extraction's entries or as an exhaustive enumeration of each kind. [concept:surface-extraction](.ok-planner/design/concepts/surface-extraction.md) says 'one entry per element the walk found' and that the extraction 'states what the walk found and how the intent classified it — nothing else', which decides neither. The nearest stated rule, 'Every universal comes back as a count and its population ... report the number checked and where the set came from' ([artifact-definitions.md](.claude/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L358)), governs audit records, not the extraction. Two open defect issues, document-catalog-per-declared-kind and document-goal-skips-catalog-completeness, fix the catalog to one file per extraction kind with rows one-to-one with the extraction; their fixes hold under every option here.

The ruling decides what completeness the catalog owes: completeness relative to the walk, or completeness over a population the extraction records.

recommendation.text:
The surface extraction commits to exhaustive enumeration per kind. For each kind it records the source it enumerated from, such as the files, registries, or declarations it read, and the count it found there, and it enumerates every member of that source. The catalog's population for each kind rests on that record, and an audit can re-enumerate a named source to refute a missed element. The story stands as written.

Rationale: the story is the owner's promise, and it promises an agent confidence in absence without reading the source. Exhaustive enumeration (B) keeps that promise, where relative completeness (A) narrows it and a named source with no promise (C) records where the set came from while committing to nothing about it. The project already answers every universal claim with a count and where the set came from, in audit records and in a subject's coverage, whose population is enumerated from the code; the catalog's 'what is not in the catalog does not exist' is such a universal, and B gives it the same shape. The extractor already visits each element to classify it, so naming the source and its count adds a record more than a walk. The flip case: if some kinds have no finite source a walk can name, such as environment variables read through computed names, exhaustiveness cannot be shown for them; C is then the honest commitment for those kinds, with the story narrowed to match.

title: The documentation catalog is complete only over what the audit's surface walk happened to find

options.label: A
options.text: Rewrite the ASCII name byte for byte in the raw bytes. Cost: a second idiom beside the core's rule that it never rewrites an undecodable file, and a wrong edit in an encoding where those bytes do not stand for the name, such as UTF-16.

options.label: B
options.text: File an intake issue for the owner and leave the file, as the caller scan does for an undecodable caller of a retired script. Cost: one more issue for the owner, on a rare file.

options.label: C
options.text: Print a `stale:` line naming the file from both check and fix, with no write and no issue. Cost: a notice the owner must act on unprompted, which every true-up repeats and nothing records.

problem:
True-up silently skips the review facts file, `.ok-planner/review/project.md`, when it does not decode as UTF-8, so a retired `.ok-review/bin/review` in that file is neither rewritten nor reported. [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) has true-up rewrite a value in owner-declared configuration that names a retired estate's path with no offer, and, for a retired script line it cannot rewrite, file an intake issue for the owner and leave the line. Rule 4.6 of [plumbline-coding.md](.claude/rules/plumbline-coding.md) says 'A caught error never ends in a bare log line or a silent default'.

The mechanism: [admin/true-up:review_config_mode](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3692) reads the file and, on `UnicodeDecodeError`, returns with no line printed ([admin/true-up](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3718)), so neither the check step's `stale:` line nor the fix step's rewrite to `.ok-planner/bin/review` happens. The stale-wording scan cannot catch it: [admin/true-up:wording_left](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2377) strips `.ok-review/bin/review` before [admin/true-up:stale_wording_lines](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L2384) looks for a retired estate path, because `review_config_mode` owns that name. The stack-lines offer names the decode failure only where `.ok-planner/config.json` declares a stack ([admin/true-up:stack_plan](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3227)), drops it for a seeded skeleton ([admin/true-up:stack_lines_offers](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L3281)), and never names the retired review tool. `/converge` pastes the review facts into every prompt, so once the retired estate is gone, an agent told to run the review tool by that path meets a missing file.

The state of play: the same core already handles an undecodable file elsewhere. Its scan for callers of a retired script classifies such a caller as kind `encoding`, 'a file that does not decode as UTF-8, so true-up cannot rewrite it byte for byte' ([admin/true-up](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L1801)), and files an intake issue for it ([admin/true-up:caller_issue](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L1925)). The built silent skip breaks rule 4.6, so keeping it is no option; the choice lies among the rest.

The ruling decides what true-up owes an owner whose review facts file does not decode.

recommendation.text:
Where the review facts file does not decode as UTF-8, true-up files an intake issue for the owner, says in its report that it filed one, and leaves the file as it stands. The issue names the file, says that true-up cannot read or rewrite it, and names the retired review tool's path and the path that replaces it.

Rationale: an intake issue with the file left is the shape the corpus already gives a retired reference true-up cannot rewrite, and the shape the same core already uses for an undecodable caller of a retired script, so the core keeps one idiom for one job (B). It ends the silent default the coding rules forbid with a record the owner works through the intake, where a `stale:` line (C) scrolls past and repeats on every true-up. A byte rewrite (A) answers with no question, and it adds a second idiom beside the never-rewrite rule and can corrupt a file in an encoding it does not read. The flip case: if undecodable review facts files prove common, one issue per project becomes noise, and true-up should instead detect the file's encoding and rewrite it in that encoding.

title: True-up says nothing when the review facts file does not decode as UTF-8, so a retired review-tool path in it stays unreported

options.label: A
options.text: Every message, people's comments and rulings included, counts as unread to each person except its author, on the command line and the dashboard; cost: unread counts grow in a busy intake several people work.

options.label: B
options.text: The story's 'whoever wrote them' means whichever agent or ceremony: the story is narrowed to say so, and only agent messages count as unread; cost: one person's answer reaches another person only when that person rereads the issue.

options.label: C
options.text: A person's ruling counts as unread to every other person, and a person's comment does not; cost: a third rule to explain, and a comment that answers a question still goes unseen.

problem:
The intake counts only agent messages as unread, so a comment or ruling one person writes never shows as new to another person, though [story:see-new-analysis](.ok-planner/design/stories/see-new-analysis.md) promises a way to see which open issues 'have new answers or revisions since I last read them, whoever wrote them'.

The intake module decides what is unread for both surfaces that show it. [issues:unread_message](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L510) counts a message only where it is a triage reply or an agent update ([issues:AGENT_TYPE_AUTHORS](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L54)). When a person reads an issue, [issues:mark_read](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L1200) sets that person's read mark to the highest agent message number ([issues:agent_mark](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/issues#L502)), not the highest message number. `issues list --unread` and the dashboard's unread tab both count through these functions. So when bob comments on an issue alice has already read, alice's `issues list --unread` prints nothing, and the dashboard's `GET /api/issues?unread=1` answers an empty list. The sprint certification of [the stack helpers sprint](.ok-planner/sprints/2026-10-15-stack-helpers.md), run converge-2026-10-16T040507, observed both.

The corpus leans two ways. The story says 'whoever wrote them'. [decision:unread-issues-count-as-new](.ok-planner/design/decisions/unread-issues-count-as-new.md) counts a never-read issue as new 'whoever filed it', and [decision:read-marks-kept-per-person](.ok-planner/design/decisions/read-marks-kept-per-person.md) keeps one ledger per person so that one person's reading never clears another's. But [decision:agent-revisions-reach-the-owner](.ok-planner/design/decisions/agent-revisions-reach-the-owner.md) commits only to agent revisions, 'whichever ceremony writes it', and says nothing of people's messages. The tooling text states the narrow behavior: [the planner's CLAUDE.md template](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/ok-planner-CLAUDE.md#L391-L392) says each triage reply and agent revision stays unread to you, and [project.md](.ok-planner/review/project.md#L33) describes `--unread` as listing open issues with agent messages you have not read.

A never-read issue and every agent message already count. Nothing counts a person's comment or ruling. Counting them takes three changes together: the unread test admits people's messages, the read mark covers every message, and a person's own messages never count as unread to that person.

The ruling decides whether a person's comment or ruling counts as unread to every other person who works the intake.

recommendation.text:
Count every message on an open issue, a person's comment or ruling included, as unread to each person except its author until that person next reads the issue, on the command line and the dashboard alike. Reading an issue marks every message on it read, not only the agent messages. A message counts once, by its number, so an edit or withdrawal of a message the reader already read does not count again. The tooling text that describes unread counts says the same.

Rationale: the story promises new answers 'whoever wrote them', and the corpus already builds for several people working one intake: [decision:read-marks-kept-per-person](.ok-planner/design/decisions/read-marks-kept-per-person.md) gives each person a ledger so that one person's reading never clears another's, and [decision:unread-issues-count-as-new](.ok-planner/design/decisions/unread-issues-count-as-new.md) counts a never-read issue as new whoever filed it. A second person's answer is the new material a shared intake exists to carry. Option B narrows the story to fit the code, and option C leaves a comment that answers a question unseen. The larger counts option A brings are the signal the story asks for. Flip case: where one owner and the agents work the intake and no second person's message ever arrives, option B costs nothing and keeps the code as it stands; where people's comments flood the unread tab in practice, option C keeps the count to rulings.

title: Another person's comment or ruling never counts as unread, only an agent's message
